content_voiceover: This chart is a classic board favorite because it visually explains why children with ALL do better than adults. Look at the childhood standard risk group on the left, the majority of that bar is high hyperdiploid and ETV6-RUNX1 fusion disease, both favorable, low-risk genetic subtypes. As you move right across childhood high risk, adolescent and young adult, and finally adult patients, that favorable purple and dark blue block shrinks dramatically, while Philadelphia chromosome positive and Philadelphia-like ALL, shown in orange and peach, expand to dominate the adult bars. Ph-like ALL in particular goes from a sliver in young children to a huge portion of the adult bar, and both Ph and Ph-like carry a worse prognosis and often require tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy. KMT2A-rearranged disease is also enriched in the childhood high-risk group, consistent with its association with infant leukemia. The exam takeaway is simple: age itself is a proxy for genetic risk, older patients are enriched for high-risk genetic lesions, which is a major reason ALL outcomes worsen with increasing age.
keypoints: High hyperdiploid and ETV6-RUNX1 fusion dominate in young children, both favorable
Ph and Ph-like ALL rise sharply with age, both high risk, need TKI therapy
KMT2A-rearranged ALL is enriched in childhood high-risk and infant cases
Age correlates with genetic risk, explaining worse ALL outcomes in adults
keypoint_voiceover: Key exam point: favorable genetics like high hyperdiploid and ETV6-RUNX1 are enriched in young children, while Philadelphia chromosome and Ph-like ALL become much more common with increasing age, and that shift explains the worsening prognosis seen from childhood to adulthood.
